blocks.note: the closing stretch of something, and here specifically of a racecourse
the surface suggests cards held in a poker hand, where a straight is a run; the setter means a race that is as good as won

explanation.surface: A card player holds the last piece of a winning set.
explanation.walkthrough: The poker picture is a decoy: once a runner reaches the last stretch before the finish, victory is in hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A racing term used figuratively: the last stretch of a course, where the finish is in sight, stands for the final stage of any task.

clue.text: Artist finding pig painting, for example, hard

blocks.note: a hog is a pig
painting is one example of art
H = hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Someone discovers that a picture of a pig was hard to make.
explanation.walkthrough: Painting is one kind of art, which is why the clue says 'for example'.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: William Hogarth was an 18th-century English painter and engraver.

clue.text: Narrow division of motorway shortened in European city

indicators.note: something shortened has lost its end, so the lane drops its last letter

blocks.note: the M1 is Britain's main north–south motorway, written MI in crosswords
a lane is a narrow division of a road; shortened, it loses its E

explanation.surface: A motorway lane is cut back somewhere in a European city.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the main motorway north out of London; setters write it MI and use 'motorway' for it.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this is Italy's second city, the capital of Lombardy.

blocks.note: to sup is to drink, and a sup is a mouthful of drink
porter is a dark beer

explanation.surface: A football fan with a drink in each hand.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark owns up to 'sup' being more a sip than a drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, in the sporting sense: the people who follow a team.

indicators.note: the word is to be judged by how it is spoken, not how it is spelt

blocks.note: natural in the sense of unprocessed, as food can be

explanation.surface: A loud noise that sounds natural to the listener.
explanation.walkthrough: This works in a British accent, where the R at the end of ROAR is not pronounced, so it sounds just like RAW.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the deep cry of a lion, or of a crowd.

indicators.note: building means putting something together, so the letters of TIED and SEMI are put together in a new form

blocks.note: fodder
fodder

explanation.surface: A heritage-listed building attached to a semi-detached house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Listed building' looks like one phrase, a protected historic building, but 'Listed' is the definition and 'building' tells you to rearrange. A semi is a semi-detached house.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: set out one item at a time, as in an itemised bill.

blocks.note: the centre or core of something
each suit in a pack of cards has thirteen cards

explanation.walkthrough: The second definition means one of the thirteen cards in the red suit of hearts.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the heart of a matter is its middle, and each card of that red suit carries the same name.

blocks.note: a judge will try, or hear, a case
the same word a second time

explanation.surface: Someone is told to keep trying and answers with enthusiasm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Try' is in the courtroom sense of trying a case.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: the cry of strong agreement heard in Parliament works as an exclamation meaning 'Absolutely!'

clue.text: More blue markings at the bottom on reptile

indicators.note: the bottom of a word is its last letter

blocks.note: the last letter of 'markings'
an adder is a snake

explanation.surface: A snake with bluer markings on its underside.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue, 'on' puts the S above the snake.
explanation.definitionFit: Blue is an idiom for low in spirits, so its comparative means more unhappy.

clue.text: Gilt edges on grail and lead pot, decorated

indicators.note: the edges of 'grail' are its first and last letters
something decorated has been dressed up and changed, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the outer letters of GRAIL
fodder

explanation.surface: A decorated chalice and pot, gilded round the rims.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gilt edges' looks like a gilded border, but 'Gilt' is the definition and 'edges on grail' gives two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a thin coating of gold over a cheaper metal.

indicators.note: 'some' of the words means only part of them, so the answer is inside

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A leader is harshly criticised over an error.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is named after the wolf in The Jungle Book and is used by Cub Scouts, so 'pack' is a Cub pack, not wolves or cards.
explanation.definitionFit: A specialised title: the adult leader of a Cub Scout pack is called by this name.

indicators.note: a name that is cut is short of its last letter

blocks.note: Arthur RANSOME, who wrote Swallows and Amazons, loses his final E

explanation.surface: A children's writer has their royalty payment reduced.
explanation.walkthrough: Arthur Ransome wrote the Swallows and Amazons books.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain definition: the sum a kidnapper demands before letting a captive go.

clue.text: Finally, document found in folder cardinal sorted

indicators.note: finally points to the last letter of 'document'
the T is found inside the other letters

blocks.note: the last letter of 'document'
a file is a folder for papers
cardinal red is the colour of a cardinal's robes

explanation.surface: An office clerk tidies a document into a folder.
explanation.walkthrough: The T does not sit inside one word but across the join of the two, which is easy to miss.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: to sort is to separate out, as a filter does with the unwanted parts.

clue.text: Tom, first in exam — magic speller?

indicators.note: first in 'exam' is its opening letter

blocks.note: a tom is a he-cat, a male cat
the first letter of 'exam'

explanation.surface: A boy named Tom comes top in a spelling test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Speller' looks like someone who spells words; here it is someone who casts spells, which the question mark flags.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Greek goddess of witchcraft is one who works magic spells.

clue.text: Agree, sovereign could be killed by this?

blocks.note: a sovereign is a British gold coin
-cide is the ending meaning killing or killer, as in regicide

explanation.surface: Someone agrees that a monarch could die this way.
explanation.walkthrough: A sovereign is a king or queen, which points toward regicide, but it is also a gold coin; read in two halves, the word would mean coin-killing.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: accounts or opinions that coincide match each other.

clue.text: Correct answer by setter suits, perhaps?

indicators.note: to correct something is to set it right, so the letters of ANSWER are set in a different order

blocks.note: the setter refers to themself as ME
fodder

explanation.surface: The setter hands in the right solution, as if dressed to suit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Correct answer' reads as the right solution, but 'Correct' is an instruction. 'By' means next to, so the setter's part may come first.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: suits are one kind of clothing for men, hence 'perhaps'.

indicators.note: mending means repairing, so the letters are worked into a new shape

blocks.note: fodder
fodder

explanation.surface: Someone repairs their trousers with glue instead of sewing.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes the pants the thing being repaired; here they are just five letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by function: a tool that fastens things together by firing staples.

clue.text: Rattling tube, get a long stick

indicators.note: things rattling are shaken about, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: fodder

explanation.surface: A tube is shaken until you get a long stick out of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stick' looks like a length of wood; in Britain a French stick is the everyday name for this loaf.
explanation.definitionFit: A regional usage: the long thin French loaf is called a French stick in Britain.

clue.text: Driver’s way off shaping solid par

indicators.note: shaping something gives it a new form, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: fodder

explanation.surface: A golfer's drive goes astray while shaping up to a solid par.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Driver' and 'par' paint a golf course, but the driver is in a car.
explanation.definitionFit: A British term: the short road by which a driver leaves or joins a motorway, called a ramp in the US.

indicators.note: the coach carries the agent inside it
in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: a coach is a kind of bus
a rep, a sales representative, is an agent

explanation.surface: A fine coach takes a travelling agent up the road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Great coach' reads as praise for a trainer, but 'Great' is the definition and the coach is a vehicle.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: excellent, first-rate.

indicators.note: the mood goes inside the baby

blocks.note: a pup is a baby dog or seal
an air is a mood or manner

explanation.surface: Parents notice a change in their baby's mood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Baby' is a young animal here, not a human infant.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as verbs: to couple is to join in twos.

blocks.note: the baseball player who throws the ball to the batter
a large jug for pouring

explanation.walkthrough: The two definitions sit side by side, with no link word between them.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the baseball player on the mound, and the large vessel with a handle and lip.

blocks.note: a tonic or drink that revives you
what someone thumbing a lift asks a driver to do

explanation.walkthrough: The second half is the phrase read literally, as words a hitch-hiker would say; the question mark flags this.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: an idiom for a tonic, and the literal plea for a lift.

clue.text: Mark scored? That may go up or down

definitions.text: That may go up or down

blocks.note: sounds like an exam result, but means a mark written in a musical score

blocks.clueFragment: That may go up or down
blocks.note: sounds like a grade that could change, but describes a word that reads the same either way, as well as a note whose stem can point up or down

explanation.surface: An exam result that could still be raised or lowered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark scored' pulls toward exams; the second half describes a palindrome, a word that reads the same up or down a column of the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a musical half note written in a score, and a palindrome, which reads the same in either direction.

blocks.note: small, not worth much thought
an insult or pointed disregard

explanation.walkthrough: One is an adjective and the other a noun (or verb), each a full definition on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: small in amount, and a deliberate insult.

blocks.note: a piece of skin or tissue moved in surgery
British informal for toil

explanation.walkthrough: The sense of hard work is everyday British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the surgical term, and a British colloquialism for toil.

clue.text: Twenty per cent off expensive asset

indicators.note: the source word has five letters, so taking twenty per cent off removes one of them

blocks.note: PLUSH, meaning expensive and luxurious, loses its last letter, one fifth of the word

explanation.surface: A discount on a costly possession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twenty per cent off' sounds like a sale, but it asks for one letter in five to go.
explanation.definitionFit: A near synonym: an advantage or good point counts as an asset.

indicators.note: to maintain is to hold, so one word holds the other

blocks.note: water ran, or flowed
a do is a party or function

explanation.surface: Gas is kept moving so that a system keeps working.
explanation.walkthrough: A do is British slang for a party or social function.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a radioactive noble gas, element 86.

clue.text: Newspaper on strike, the broadcast claims

the scrambled THE claims, or takes in, the other letters

blocks.note: in cricket the on side is also called the leg side
a rap is a sharp strike
fodder

explanation.walkthrough: 'On strike' looks like a phrase about industrial action, but the two words work separately. The on side in cricket is the half of the field behind the batter's legs.

clue.text: One taking someone off in spare motor, breaking down

blocks.note: fodder

explanation.surface: Someone gives a lift in a spare car that then breaks down.
